accepted.label: Bag-of-Words Model Definition
accepted.description: The bag-of-words (BOW) model is a text representation technique that converts documents into fixed-length vectors by counting word occurrences, disregarding grammar and word order. It treats a document as an unordered collection of words.
coverage_criteria: Define the BOW model and explain how it represents text as word count vectors.
Identify that BOW disregards word order and context.
accepted.merge_rationale: These candidates all define the BOW model as a text representation based on word frequency, ignoring order, forming a single teachable concept.

accepted.label: Vocabulary Construction in Bag-of-Words
accepted.description: The vocabulary is the set of all unique words across the document corpus. It determines the dimensions of the BOW vectors. Each document is represented as a vector of length equal to the vocabulary size, where each position corresponds to a specific word.
coverage_criteria: Define what the vocabulary is in BOW.
Explain how the vocabulary determines vector size and how out-of-vocabulary words are handled.
accepted.merge_rationale: These candidates all focus on the concept of vocabulary in BOW: its construction, its role in defining vector dimensions, and its impact on encoding.

accepted.label: BOW Vectorization Process
accepted.description: The BOW vectorization process consists of determining the vocabulary (collecting unique words) and then counting the occurrences of each vocabulary word in each document to produce a count vector.
coverage_criteria: List the steps for BOW vectorization (vocabulary construction and counting).
Apply counting to convert a small document into a BOW vector.
accepted.merge_rationale: These candidates describe the procedural steps of BOW vectorization, emphasizing the two core stages: vocabulary definition and word counting.

accepted.label: Loss of Word Order and Context in BOW
accepted.description: BOW discards the order of words, meaning it cannot capture syntax or semantics that depend on word sequence. This loss of contextual information is a fundamental limitation of the model.
coverage_criteria: State that BOW does not preserve word order.
Provide an example of how meaning can be lost due to ignoring word order.
accepted.merge_rationale: These candidates all highlight that BOW functions like a literal bag of words, losing positional and contextual information, which is a key drawback.

accepted.label: Implementing BOW with Keras Tokenizer
accepted.description: In Python, the Keras Tokenizer class can be used to implement BOW. After fitting on texts to build the vocabulary, texts_to_matrix with mode='count' generates count vectors.
coverage_criteria: Write Python code to use Keras Tokenizer for BOW vectorization.
Explain the roles of fit_on_texts and texts_to_matrix.
accepted.merge_rationale: These candidates demonstrate the implementation of BOW using the Keras Tokenizer API, a practical skill for the lesson.

accepted.label: Applications and Strengths of BOW
accepted.description: Despite its simplicity, BOW is effective for tasks like text classification and profanity detection. Its strengths are simplicity and low computational cost.
coverage_criteria: Name two NLP applications where BOW is useful.
Explain why BOW's simplicity can be advantageous.
accepted.merge_rationale: These candidates discuss the practical uses and benefits of BOW, providing context for why the model is still relevant.

accepted.label: Text Preprocessing: Tokenization and Stopword Removal
accepted.description: Tokenization splits text into individual words (tokens). Stopwords are common low-information words that are often removed to reduce noise and vocabulary size. NLTK provides built-in stopword lists.
coverage_criteria: Define tokenization and stopword removal.
Write code to remove stopwords using NLTK.
accepted.merge_rationale: These candidates cover the preprocessing steps essential for BOW: tokenizing text and removing stopwords, which are often taught together.

accepted.label: Sparse Vectors Problem
accepted.description: When the vocabulary is large, BOW vectors become mostly zeros (sparse), leading to high memory usage and computational inefficiency.
coverage_criteria: Define a sparse vector in the context of BOW.
Explain why sparsity is a challenge for machine learning.
accepted.merge_rationale: This candidate represents a distinct limitation of BOW related to vector sparsity, worthy of its own concept.

accepted.label: Implementing BOW from Scratch in Python
accepted.description: BOW can be implemented manually by writing functions to tokenize, remove stopwords, build a vocabulary, and generate count vectors using basic Python and NumPy.
coverage_criteria: Describe the key components of a from-scratch BOW implementation.
Write a simple function to generate a BOW vector from text.
accepted.merge_rationale: This candidate provides a detailed manual implementation of BOW, which helps understand the underlying mechanics.

accepted.label: Using Scikit-learn's CountVectorizer for BOW
accepted.description: Scikit-learn's CountVectorizer offers a ready-to-use BOW implementation with parameters for preprocessing, tokenization, n-grams, and more, outputting a term-document matrix.
coverage_criteria: Instantiate CountVectorizer with common parameters.
Apply fit_transform to a list of texts and interpret the output.
accepted.merge_rationale: These candidates introduce CountVectorizer and its parameters, a practical tool for BOW in the scikit-learn ecosystem.

accepted.label: N-gram Extension to Bag-of-Words
accepted.description: BOW can be extended to n-grams (e.g., bigrams) where tokens are sequences of n consecutive words, partially capturing word order.
coverage_criteria: Define an n-gram and give an example of bigrams.
Explain how n-grams address the loss-of-order limitation.
accepted.merge_rationale: This candidate presents an important extension to basic BOW that captures some word order, adding depth to the lesson.

accepted.label: Why Text Needs to Be Converted to Numbers for Machine Learning
accepted.description: Machine learning algorithms require numerical input (matrices). Text data must be vectorized into feature vectors so that models can learn a mapping Y=f(X).
coverage_criteria: Explain the necessity of numerical representation for ML models.
Describe the Y=f(X) formulation and the role of vectorization.
accepted.merge_rationale: These candidates provide the foundational motivation for text vectorization, essential context for the BOW method.

accepted.label: Binary Bag-of-Words Encoding
accepted.description: In binary BOW, a sentence is represented by a binary vector where each dimension indicates the presence (1) or absence (0) of a vocabulary word, rather than its count.
coverage_criteria: Differentiate between count-based and binary BOW.
Given a vocabulary and a sentence, produce a binary BOW vector.
accepted.merge_rationale: This candidate introduces a specific encoding variant (binary/presence-based) of BOW, which is a distinct teachable sub-concept.

accepted.label: Natural Language Challenges
accepted.description: Natural language is inherently structured yet free-form; the same meaning can be expressed in many ways, and similar words can convey different meanings, making NLP distinct from other data types.
coverage_criteria: Give examples of sentences where similar words convey different meanings, and explain why NLP requires special approaches compared to tabular data.
accepted.merge_rationale: Single candidate covering foundational NLP challenge.

accepted.label: Multi-label Encoding with Binary Vectors
accepted.description: In multi-label classification, labels are encoded as binary vectors where each index corresponds to a label, allowing a single example to have multiple 1s, unlike one-hot encoding for multi-class.
coverage_criteria: Encode a set of labels for a given text using a binary vector, and contrast with one-hot encoding for multi-class.
accepted.merge_rationale: Single candidate covering label encoding for multi-label tasks.

accepted.label: Sigmoid Activation for Multi-label Classification
accepted.description: For multi-label text classification with a bag-of-words model, the output layer should use sigmoid activation with binary cross-entropy loss, as it allows independent binary predictions per label, while softmax is for multi-class.
coverage_criteria: Explain why sigmoid activation is preferred over softmax for multi-label classification, and select the appropriate loss function.
accepted.merge_rationale: Single candidate covering model output configuration for multi-label.

accepted.label: HashVectorizer: Hashing-based Vectorization
accepted.description: Scikit-learn's HashVectorizer applies a hash function to map terms to numerical indices, saving memory but making it impossible to recover original feature names, unlike CountVectorizer.
coverage_criteria: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage of using HashVectorizer compared to CountVectorizer.
accepted.merge_rationale: Single candidate introducing HashVectorizer as an alternative vectorizer.

accepted.label: TfidfVectorizer: TF-IDF Weighting
accepted.description: Scikit-learn's TfidfVectorizer assigns weights to terms combining term frequency (TF) and inverse document frequency (IDF), giving higher importance to discriminative terms across the corpus, unlike simple count-based BoW.
coverage_criteria: Define TF-IDF and explain how it differs from simple count-based vectorization.
accepted.merge_rationale: Single candidate introducing TfidfVectorizer as an alternative weighting method.
